pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 7-9 (Lower KS2/Grades 2-4): the insect body plan — three body parts (head, thorax, abdomen), six legs attached to the THORAX, antennae on the head, most have wings, and an exoskeleton (hard outer shell) instead of internal bones.
• Standards — UK (DfE): KS2 Y4 'Living things and their habitats' (grouping by observable features; classification). Builds the shared body plan that the 'is it an insect?' and classification-key topics depend on.
• Standards — US (NGSS): 1-LS1-1 (external parts) extended; supports 3-LS4 diversity/classification reasoning.
• Operational details — the load-bearing facts are the count (6 legs, 3 parts) and WHERE they attach (legs on the thorax). Use real specimens/large photos and get children to label and count. Introduce exoskeleton by contrast with our internal skeleton (armour on the outside). This is the definitional backbone for later sorting — precision matters.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 7): labels head, thorax, abdomen on an insect diagram. Tier B (age 8): states 'six legs, attached to the thorax' and that insects have an exoskeleton not bones. Tier C (age 9): uses the body plan as a rule to justify whether a creature is an insect ('6 legs and 3 parts, so yes').
bestPractices: Make the count and location load-bearing: 'six legs, all attached to the thorax' — children must know WHERE, not just how many.
Use real specimens or large clear photos and have children label and count for themselves.
Introduce exoskeleton by direct contrast with our internal skeleton (armour on the outside vs bones inside).
Treat the body plan as the definitional rule they will apply later to sort insects from non-insects — insist on precision now.
Address 'most have wings' carefully — wings are common but not the defining feature; the six legs and three parts are.
keyRepresentations: A large labelled insect diagram/photo (head, thorax, abdomen; legs on thorax; antennae).
An exoskeleton-vs-endoskeleton comparison (beetle armour vs human x-ray).
A leg-count highlight (count to six along the thorax).
A 'build a valid insect' assembly tray.
commonMisconceptions: 'Spiders are insects' — spiders have 8 legs and 2 body parts; the six-legs/three-parts rule excludes them.
'Insects have bones' — they have an exoskeleton, not an internal skeleton.
'Legs come from all over the body' — all six attach to the thorax specifically.
'All insects have wings / anything with wings is an insect' — wings are common but not defining.
'Any small crawly thing is an insect' — the term is precise, not a synonym for 'bug' or 'minibeast'.

learn.summary: For ages 7-9 (Lower KS2 / Grades 2-4): the insect body plan. Adult insects have three body parts (head, thorax, abdomen), exactly six legs that all attach to the thorax, usually one pair of antennae on the head, and a hard outer exoskeleton instead of internal bones. Most adult insects also have wings. The load-bearing facts are the count (six legs, three parts) and the location (legs attach to the thorax). This becomes the main rule children use to recognise an adult insect (young stages such as caterpillars or maggots can look different).

activities.title: Label and count on a real insect
feedback: If a learner traces a leg to the abdomen or head, invite them to follow it again on the real specimen/photo: every leg meets the body at the middle segment.
If they count other than six, have them count aloud touching each leg once; confirm six (if a real specimen is damaged and missing a leg, point out where it would have been).
Reinforce the thorax as 'the part the legs and wings come from' so location is attached to the name, not just memorised.
activities.rationale: Using a real specimen or large photo and having children label and count for themselves makes the count and location load-bearing rather than a recited list. A fixed labelled diagram can present the plan clearly; counting and tracing on an actual specimen adds the learner's own verification. A real specimen may vary (damaged legs, folded wings), so treat the labelled plan as the ideal rule.
sourceClaims: Insects are defined by three tagmata (head, thorax, abdomen), six legs attached to the thorax, typically one pair of antennae, and an exoskeleton.
learnerActions: Look closely at a real specimen or a large, clear photo of a beetle or bee.
Point to and label the three body parts: head (front), thorax (middle), abdomen (back).
Count the legs one by one, 1 through 6, and trace each leg back to where it joins the body.
State out loud: 'Six legs, and they all attach to the thorax — the middle part.'
Find and name the antennae on the head; point to where the wings attach (the thorax).
activities.intendedInsight: An insect has three body parts and exactly six legs, and all six legs (and the wings) attach to the thorax specifically — not the head or abdomen.

activities.title: Bones inside or shell outside?
feedback: If a learner says the insect has bones inside, contrast directly: feel your own arm bone inside, then handle/examine the beetle's hard outer shell. The support is on the outside.
If they treat 'skeleton' as always internal, name exoskeleton = 'outside skeleton' and point to where it is.
Prompt: 'Why does the beetle need that hard outer shell?' to check they grasp external support, not just repeat the word.
activities.rationale: Introducing exoskeleton by direct contrast with our internal skeleton targets the common misconception that insects have bones inside, and the 'why does it need that?' probe checks whether the learner grasps that support can be external rather than importing the human body plan.
sourceClaims: Insects are defined by three tagmata (head, thorax, abdomen), six legs attached to the thorax, typically one pair of antennae, and an exoskeleton.
learnerActions: Feel an arm or leg and notice the hard bone is on the INSIDE of the body.
Look at a beetle shell or a shed exoskeleton (or a close-up photo) and notice the hard part is on the OUTSIDE.
Compare a human x-ray picture (skeleton inside) with the beetle's armour (skeleton outside).
Say in your own words: 'An exoskeleton is a skeleton on the outside — a hard shell that holds the insect's shape and protects it.'
Answer: if an insect has no bones inside, what holds its shape? (Its exoskeleton.)
activities.intendedInsight: Support and protection can come from a hard covering on the OUTSIDE (exoskeleton), not only from bones on the inside; insects use an exoskeleton instead of an internal skeleton.

activities.title: Build a valid insect / apply the rule
feedback: If a learner attaches legs to the abdomen or adds an extra pair, point out which rule is broken and have them move the legs to the thorax / remove the extra pair.

If they count only two body parts (merging head+thorax or thorax+abdomen), use a three-segment or three-bead model — front (head), middle (thorax, where legs join), back (abdomen) — and count three each time.
Praise correct justification that names BOTH the count and the location.
activities.rationale: An assembly or rule-checking task gives active reinforcement and asks the learner to construct, not just recognise, the plan, and then transfer it to classify. The spider counterexample addresses the 'spiders are insects' misconception by contrasting 8 legs / 2 parts.
sourceClaims: KS2 Y4 requires pupils to explore and use classification to group living things by observable features, for which the insect body plan is the definitional basis.
learnerActions: Assemble a model insect from parts: one head, one thorax, one abdomen, joined front-to-back.
Attach exactly six legs — all to the thorax (middle part).
Check your build against the rule: three parts, six legs, legs on the thorax.
Test whether other creatures fit the rule: a spider has 8 legs and 2 body parts, with legs coming off the front part — is it built the same way? (No — not an insect.)
Explain your decision: 'It has six legs and three parts, legs on the thorax, so it is an insect' — or why something is not.
activities.intendedInsight: The body plan works as a recognition rule: an adult insect has three parts and six legs attached to the thorax, so a creature that breaks the rule, like a spider with 8 legs and 2 body parts, is not an insect.

constraints: Precision matters: insist on both the count (six legs, three parts) AND the location (legs attach to the thorax), not just how many.

Handle 'most have wings' carefully — wings are common but NOT the defining feature. The six legs and three parts (with legs on the thorax) are the key features used at this level to recognise an adult insect.
Keep the term 'insect' precise — it is not a synonym for 'bug' or 'minibeast'. Any small crawly thing is not automatically an insect.

Labelling, leg-count, and fill-the-blank questions assess the definitional facts but only check recognition/recall; they do not by themselves require the learner to construct the plan or justify a classification. Pair them with a build or explanation task.
A labelled picture or model shows a fixed, idealised plan; real specimens vary (damaged legs, folded wings). Use the ideal plan as the rule and note that real specimens may be imperfect.

Tap-to-reveal regions (e.g. select a segment to highlight it and show captions, count legs by selecting each) are optional ways to make the plan concrete; they are not required, and spoken explanation plus the 'why?' probe remain valuable.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources have NOT been re-fetched or re-verified. Both source claims are marked verified:false in the row. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original material notes 'typically/one pair of antennae' and 'most have wings'; retained as typical, not universal, to avoid overstating. Some insect groups differ, but at this age the shared plan is taught as the rule.

The original listed an open-dialogue format as a poor fit for fixed vocabulary; this is a catalog-fit judgement, not an established pedagogical law, so it has been dropped rather than asserted as a universal limit. Spoken explanation and the 'why?' probe are still valuable during teaching.

A prerequisite reteach link (internal identifier) referenced for the leg-attachment misconception is preserved conceptually but the internal identifier is omitted; a reviewer should confirm the intended prerequisite topic.

probeDeeper: 'You said six legs. Where exactly do they all join — the head, the middle, or the back?'
'A spider has its legs coming off the front part and has eight of them. Is a spider built the same way as this beetle, or differently?' (arachnid counterexample)
'If an insect has no bones inside, what stops it from being squishy — what holds its shape?'
'Point to where the wings would attach. Head, thorax, or abdomen?'
assess.correctAnswer: The beetle has three body parts: head (at the front, with the antennae), thorax (the middle), and abdomen (the back). It has exactly six legs, and they all attach to the thorax (the middle part), never to the head or abdomen. A beetle has no bones inside — it has an exoskeleton, a hard outer shell on the outside, which protects and supports its body.

errorPatterns.pattern: Attaches legs to the abdomen or spreads them along the whole body, rather than all six to the thorax
errorPatterns.nextMove: Look at a real beetle or a large clear photo and trace each leg back to where it joins — all to the middle. Name the thorax as 'the part the legs and wings come from'.
errorPatterns.distractor: The legs are spread out all along the body
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Draws or points to legs coming off the back/abdomen; can't identify the thorax as the leg-bearing segment

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks the insect has a skeleton/bones inside like a human — imports the human body plan onto the insect
errorPatterns.nextMove: Handle a shed exoskeleton or beetle shell — show the hard support is on the OUTSIDE. Contrast with feeling their own arm bone inside. Name exoskeleton = 'outside skeleton'.
errorPatterns.distractor: It has bones inside, like we do
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Second tier: says the beetle has bones inside, or doesn't know what holds it up; treats 'skeleton' as always internal

errorPatterns.pattern: Merges head and thorax (or thorax and abdomen) into one — counts only two body parts
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use a three-bead or three-segment model and match to the beetle: front (head), middle (thorax, where legs join), back (abdomen). Count three every time.
errorPatterns.distractor: An insect has two body parts — a head and a body
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Names only 'head and body'; cannot separate thorax from abdomen

responseLevels.gap: Miscounts legs, attaches them to the wrong part, or says the insect has bones inside; body parts not separable.
responseLevels.full: Labels all three parts, attaches all six legs to the thorax, explains the exoskeleton is a hard OUTER covering that supports the body, AND transfers the plan — e.g. contrasts a spider's 8 legs / 2 parts as built differently.
responseLevels.partial: Names head/thorax/abdomen and says six legs, but as a memorised list — can't reliably attach the legs to the thorax specifically, or can't explain the exoskeleton as external support.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is a picture of a beetle. Point to its head, its thorax, and its abdomen, and tell me how many legs it has and where they attach. Then tell me: does a beetle have bones inside like we do, or something else — and why does it need that?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who has the body plan attaches all six legs to the THORAX and names the exoskeleton as an outer covering. A child with a fuzzy picture spreads legs along the whole body, miscounts, or says the beetle has bones/a skeleton inside like a person — the second-tier 'why does it need that?' exposes whether they grasp that support can be external, or whether they are just importing the human body plan onto the insect.
